{{Short description|The log of the S-matrix in scattering}}

<!--{{Orphan|date=August 2026}}-->
In [[Scattering#Theoretical physics|scattering theory]], the '''scattering generator''' or '''''S''-generator''' is an effective [[Hamiltonian (quantum mechanics)|Hamiltonian]] that directly generates the [[interaction picture|interaction-picture]] time evolution from far past to far future.

In [[quantum mechanics]] and [[quantum field theory]], the scattering generator is the log of the [[S-matrix|''S''-matrix]]: <math>\hat{\Omega} = i\hbar \log\hat{S}</math>. While the concept traces back to '80s,
an active revival has taken place in the modern literature<ref name=Amplitudes2026TalkShi>{{Cite speech
|last=Shi |first=Canxin 
|date=May 29, 2026 
|title=Classical scattering from QFT via phase space dequantization
|url=https://indico.global/event/16407/contributions/152356/attachments/73189/141877/Canxin-Shi.pdf
|event=Amplitudes 2026 Conference
|location=Queen Mary University of London
 }}</ref><ref name=Amplitudes2026TalkBrown>{{Cite speech
|last=Brown |first=Graham 
|date=May 29, 2026 
|title=The Magnus Expansion in QFT
|url=https://indico.global/event/16407/contributions/152357/attachments/73190/141878/Graham_Brown.pdf
|event=Amplitudes 2026 Conference
|location=Queen Mary University of London
 }}</ref> on scattering theory and its applications. In [[classical mechanics]], the classical scattering generator describes the Hamiltonian generator of the
''S''-symplectomorphism, which is the classical analog of the [[S-matrix|''S''-matrix]]. The quantum and classical scattering generators
are related by the [[classical limit]] by a precise correspondence.<ref name="PSFOR">{{Cite arXiv|last=Kim |first=Joonhwi |date=2025 |title=Phase space formulation of S-matrix |class=hep-th |eprint=2512.23100 }}</ref>

== History and Motivation ==

=== Exponential representation of ''S''-matrix ===

The idea of taking the log of ''S''-matrix
traces back to early days of [[quantum field theory]]<ref name=OLD1>{{Cite journal
|first1= Richard P. |last1= Feynman
|title= An Operator calculus having applications in quantum electrodynamics
|journal= Phys. Rev. 
|date= 1951
|volume=  84
|pages=  108–128
|url= https://journals.aps.org/pr/abstract/10.1103/PhysRev.84.108
|doi= 10.1103/PhysRev.84.108
|bibcode= 1951PhRv...84..108F
}}</ref><ref name=OLD2>{{Cite journal
|first1= H. |last1= Lehmann
|first2= K. |last2= Symanzik
|first3= W. |last3= Zimmermann
|title= On the formulation of quantized field theories. II
|journal= Nuovo Cim. 
|date= 1957
|volume=  6
|issue=  2
|pages= 319–333
|url= https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF02832508
|doi= 10.1007/BF02832508
|bibcode= 1957NCim....6..319L
|url-access= subscription
}}</ref>
and has been known as the [[Exponential map (Lie theory)|exponential representation]]
of [[S-matrix|''S''-matrix]], which refers to the formula<ref name=Damgaard>
{{Cite journal 
|last1=Damgaard |first1=Poul H.
|last2=Hansen |first2=Elias Roos
|last3=Planté |first3=Ludovic 
|last4=Vanhove |first4=Pierre
|date=2023
|title=Classical observables from the exponential representation of the gravitational S-matrix
|journal=Journal of High Energy Physics
|volume= 
|issue= 9
|article-number=183
|url=https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/JHEP09(2023)183
|doi=10.1007/JHEP09(2023)183
|arxiv=2307.04746
|bibcode=2023JHEP...09..183D
}}
</ref><math display="block">
\begin{aligned}
\hat{S} \,=\, \exp\bigg(\frac{1}{i\hbar}\, \hat{\Omega}\bigg)
\,.
\end{aligned}
</math>

=== Exponential representation as unit-time flow ===
Modern literature interprets <math>\hat{\Omega}</math> as the unit-time generator of scattering,<ref name=2405.17056>
{{Cite journal 
|last1=Kim |first1=Joonhwi
|last2=Kim |first2=Jung-Wook
|last3=Lee |first3=Sangmin
|date=2024
|title=Massive twistor worldline in electromagnetic fields
|journal=Journal of High Energy Physics
|volume= 
|issue= 8
|article-number=80
|url=https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/JHEP08(2024)080
|doi=10.1007/JHEP08(2024)080
|arxiv=2405.17056
|bibcode=2024JHEP...08..080K
}}</ref><ref name=Gonzo-Shi>
{{Cite journal 
|last1=Gonzo |first1=Riccardo
|last2=Shi |first2=Canxin
|date=2024
|title=Scattering and Bound Observables for Spinning Particles in Kerr Spacetime with Generic Spin Orientations
|journal=Phys. Rev. Lett.
|volume=133
|issue=22
|article-number=221401
|url=https://journals.aps.org/prl/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevLett.133.221401
|doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.133.221401
|pmid=39672109
|arxiv=2405.09687
|bibcode=2024PhRvL.133v1401G
}}</ref> while prototypical observations trace back to the '80s.{{#tag:ref|
"The quasiclassical phase shift is identified as the generator of the classical canonical S transformation."<ref name=OLD6>
{{Cite journal |last1=Narnhofer |first1=H. |last2=Thirring |first2=W. | title=Canonical scattering transformation in classical mechanics |volume=23 |issue=4 |date=1981 |journal=Physical Review A
|pages=1688–1697 |url =https://journals.aps.org/pra/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevA.23.1688
|doi =10.1103/PhysRevA.23.1688
|bibcode=1981PhRvA..23.1688N }}</ref>
|name:NoteNT}} The above formula is viewed
as an effective [[time evolution]] through dimensionless unit time:<math display="block">
\begin{aligned}
\hat{S} \,=\, 
\exp\bigg(\frac{(\text{“}\mathit{\Delta}t = 1\text{”})}{i\hbar}\, \hat{\Omega}\bigg)
\,.
\end{aligned}
</math>This means that the result of scattering <math>\hat{S}</math> is directly reproduced within "one second" (<math>\mathit{\Delta}t = 1</math>) by taking <math>\hat{\Omega}</math> as the [[Hamiltonian (quantum mechanics)|Hamiltonian]].<ref name=CS />
In this sense, <math>\hat{\Omega}</math> is viewed as an "effective Hamiltonian" that encapsulates and summarizes
the entire history of scattering from <math>t=-\infty</math> to <math>t=+\infty</math>.

=== Manifest unitarity ===

The motivation behind the exponential representation is manifest [[unitarity]] in scattering, i.e., trivializing the conservation of probability. Provided hermiticity <math>\hat{\Omega}^\dagger = \hat{\Omega}</math>,the ''S''-matrix is automatically unitary as<math display="block">
\begin{aligned}
\hat{S}^\dagger \hat{S} \,=\, \exp\bigg({-\frac{1}{i\hbar}\, \hat{\Omega}}\bigg)
\exp\bigg(\frac{1}{i\hbar}\, \hat{\Omega}\bigg)
\,=\,
\hat{1}
\,.
\end{aligned}
</math>This also applies for the classical scattering generator as well, the conservation of classical probability in the sense of [[Liouville's theorem (Hamiltonian)|Liouville theorem]].<ref name=CS>
{{Cite journal
|last=Kim |first=Joonhwi
|title=Manifest symplecticity in classical scattering
|journal=Journal of High Energy Physics
|date=2026
|volume=
|issue=5
|article-number=287
|doi=10.1007/JHEP05(2026)287
|arxiv=2511.07387
|bibcode=2026JHEP...05..287K
}}</ref>

== Definition by Magnus Expansion ==
The [[S-matrix|''S''-matrix]] is concretely defined and computed by the [[Dyson series]],
which expands a [[path-ordered exponential|time-ordered exponential]].The scattering generator is concretely defined and computed by
the [[Magnus series]].<ref name=KKKL>
{{Cite journal 
|last1=Kim |first1=Joonhwi
|last2=Kim |first2=Jung-Wook
|last3=Kim |first3=Sungsoo
|last4=Lee |first4=Sangmin
|date=2024
|title=Classical eikonal from Magnus expansion
|journal=Journal of High Energy Physics
|volume=01
|article-number=111
|doi=10.1007/JHEP01(2025)111
|doi-access=free
}}</ref>

=== In quantum mechanics ===

For the quantum scattering generator <math>\hat{\Omega}</math>, the Magnus series formula reads<ref name=KKKL/><math display="block">
\begin{aligned}
\hat{\Omega}
\,=\,
{}&{}
\int dt_1\,\,
			\hat{V}_\text{I}(t_1)
+
		\frac{1}{2(i\hbar)^1}
		\int_{t_1>t_2} d^2t\,\,
			[\hat V_\text{I}(t_1),\hat V_\text{I}(t_2)]
\\
{}&{}
+
		\frac{1}{6(i\hbar)^2}
		\int_{t_1>t_2>t_3} d^3t\,\,
			\Big(\,{
				[ \hat V_\text{I}(t_1) , [ \hat V_\text{I}(t_2) , \hat V_\text{I}(t_3) ] ]
				+
				[ \hat V_\text{I}(t_3) , [ \hat V_\text{I}(t_2) , \hat V_\text{I}(t_1) ] ]
			}\,\Big)
+ \cdots
\,.
\end{aligned}
</math>This describes a sum of integrals whose integrands are nested commutators between the [[interaction picture|interaction-picture]] potential <math>\hat{V}_\mathrm{I}(t)</math> at different times. Provided the free and interaction Hamiltonians are Hermitian, the scattering generator <math>\hat{\Omega}</math> is also a Hermitian operator.

=== In classical mechanics ===

For the classical scattering generator <math>\Omega</math>, the Magnus series formula reads<math display="block">
\begin{aligned}
\Omega
\,=\,
{}&{}
\int dt_1\,\,
			V_\text{I}(t_1)
+
		\frac{1}{2}
		\int_{t_1>t_2} d^2t\,\,
			\{V_\text{I}(t_1),V_\text{I}(t_2)\}
\\
{}&{}
+
		\frac{1}{6}
		\int_{t_1>t_2>t_3} d^3t\,\,
			\Big(\,{
				\{ V_\text{I}(t_1) , \{ V_\text{I}(t_2) , V_\text{I}(t_3) \} \}
				+
				\{ V_\text{I}(t_3) , \{ V_\text{I}(t_2) , V_\text{I}(t_1) \} \}
			}\,\Big)
+ \cdots
\,,
\end{aligned}
</math>which can be deduced by taking the [[classical limit]] to the above quantum formula
n spirit of  the [[correspondence principle]] and [[Canonical quantization#Classical and quantum brackets|canonical quantization]].<ref name=KKKL/>
This assumes a [[Hamiltonian mechanics|Hamiltonian system]] defined on a [[phase space]] equipped with a [[Poisson bracket]]. <math>\Omega</math> is a function on the phase space. <math>V_\text{I}(t)</math> is a time-dependent function on the phase space,
encoding the classical interaction Hamiltonian in the [[interaction picture]].

More precisely, the frameworks of [[phase space formulation]] and [[deformation quantization]]
have been employed to establish the relationship between
<math>\hat{\Omega}</math> and <math>\Omega</math>
in a rigorous fashion.<ref name=PSFOR/> The classical scattering generator is well-defined on [[Poisson manifold]]s.<ref name=CS/>

The ''S''-symplectomorphism <math>S</math>,
i.e., the canonical transformation from the initial phase space to the final phase space
in classical scattering, arises by exponentiating the [[Hamiltonian vector field]] of  <math>\Omega</math>.{{#tag:ref|
The precise equation is
<math>S^* = \exp(\{\Omega,\,\,\,\})</math>,
which provides
the [[Exponential map (Lie theory)|exponential representation]]
for the pullback <math>S^*</math> of the [[S-symplectomorphism#Symplectic property|''S''-symplectomorphism]].
In turn, one could write <math>\{\Omega,\,\,\,\} = \log S^*</math>.
|note:NoteS*}}

== Use ==

=== In quantum mechanics ===

In the [[interaction picture]], the [[quantum Liouville equation]]
reads
<math display="block">
\begin{aligned}
\frac{d}{dt}\, \hat{\rho}_\mathrm{I}(t)
\,=\,
   \frac{1}{i\hbar}\,[
      \hat{V}_\mathrm{I}(t),
      \hat{\rho}_\mathrm{I}(t)
   ]
\,,
\end{aligned}
</math>
where <math>\hat{\rho}_\mathrm{I}(t)</math>
is the [[density matrix]] in the [[interaction picture]]. Solving this equation gives rise to the [[S-matrix|''S''-matrix]] <math>\hat{S}</math> as
<math display="block">
\begin{aligned}
\hat{\rho}_\mathrm{I}(+\infty)
\,=\,
    \hat{S}\, \hat{\rho}_\mathrm{I}(-\infty)\, \hat{S}{}^{-1}
\,=\,
    \mathrm{Ad}_{\hat{S}}\, \hat{\rho}_\mathrm{I}(-\infty)
\,,
\end{aligned}
</math>in terms of the [[adjoint action]] <math>\mathrm{Ad}_{\hat{S}}</math>.
The formula <math>\hat{S} = e^{\hat{\Omega}/i\hbar}</math> then implies
<math display="block">
\begin{aligned}
\hat{\rho}_\mathrm{I}(+\infty)
\,&=\,
   \exp\Big(\,{
      \mathrm{ad}_{\hat{\Omega}/i\hbar}
   }\,\Big)\, \hat{\rho}_\mathrm{I}(-\infty)
\,,\\
\,&=\,
   \exp\bigg(\,{
      \frac{1}{i\hbar}\, [ \hat{\Omega} , \,\,\, ]
   }\,\bigg)\, \hat{\rho}_\mathrm{I}(-\infty)
\,,\\
\,&=\,
   \hat{\rho}_\mathrm{I}(-\infty)
+ \frac{1}{i\hbar}\, [\hat{\Omega},\hat{\rho}_\mathrm{I}(-\infty)]
+ \frac{1}{2!(i\hbar)^2}\, [\hat{\Omega},[\hat{\Omega},\hat{\rho}_\mathrm{I}(-\infty)]]
+ \cdots
\,,
\end{aligned}
</math>which describes a sum of nested commutators.

This describes that the entire time evolution of the quantum ([[Ensemble (mathematical physics)|ensemble]]) state
from <math>\hat{\rho}_\mathrm{I}(-\infty)</math>
to <math>\hat{\rho}_\mathrm{I}(+\infty)</math>
is reproduced by a unit-time, [[Exponential map (Lie theory)|exponentiated]] [[adjoint action]]
of the scattering generator <math>\hat{\Omega}</math>.

=== In classical mechanics ===

In classical [[Hamiltonian mechanics]], an analogous formula holds for the 
classical probability [[Distribution function (physics)|distribution]]
<math>\rho(t)</math>,
representing a [[Ensemble (mathematical physics)|statistical ensemble]]
and evolving under the classical [[Liouville's theorem (Hamiltonian)#Liouville equation|Liouville equation]]:<ref name=PSFOR /><math display="block">
\begin{aligned}
\rho_\mathrm{I}(+\infty)
\,&=\,
   \exp\Big(\,{
      \{ \Omega , \,\,\, \}
   }\,\Big)\, {\rho}_\mathrm{I}(-\infty)
\,,\\
\,&=\,
   {\rho}_\mathrm{I}(-\infty)
+ \{{\Omega},{\rho}_\mathrm{I}(-\infty)\}
+ \frac{1}{2!}\, \{{\Omega},\{{\Omega},{\rho}_\mathrm{I}(-\infty)\}\}
+ \cdots
\,.
\end{aligned}
</math>This is the nested Poisson bracket formula in the [[S-symplectomorphism|''S''-symplectomorphism]] framework.

=== Impulse formula ===

In quantum mechanics, the expectation value of an observable <math>\hat{\mathcal{O}}</math> with respect to the density matrix
<math>\hat{\rho}_\text{I}(t)</math> in the interaction picture is<math display="block">
\begin{aligned}
\big\langle
\hat{\mathcal{O}}
\big\rangle_t
\,=\,
\mathrm{Tr}\big(\,\hat{\rho}_\text{I}(t)\,\hat{\mathcal{O}}\,\big)
\,.
\end{aligned}
</math>The impulse of observables in quantum scattering is<math display="block">
\begin{aligned}
\big\langle
\hat\mathcal{O}
\big\rangle_{+\infty}
-
\big\langle
\hat\mathcal{O}
\big\rangle_{-\infty}
\,&=\,
   e^{[\,\,\,\,,\hat{\Omega}/i\hbar]}
\hat\mathcal{O}
-\hat\mathcal{O}
\,=\,
\frac{1}{i\hbar}\, [\hat\mathcal{O},\hat{\Omega}]
+ \frac{1}{2!(i\hbar)^2}\, [[\hat\mathcal{O},\hat{\Omega}],\hat{\Omega}]
+ \cdots
\,.
\end{aligned}
</math>In classical mechanics, the expectation value of an observable <math>\mathcal{O}</math> with respect to the probability distribution
<math>\rho_\text{I}(t)</math>
in the interaction picture is<math display="block">
\begin{aligned}
\big\langle
\mathcal{O}
\big\rangle_t
\,=\,
\int \rho_\text{I}(t)\, \mathcal{O}\,\, \mu
\,,
\end{aligned}
</math>where <math>\mu</math> is the Liouville measure.
The impulse of observables in classical scattering is then<math display="block">
\begin{aligned}
\big\langle
\mathcal{O}
\big\rangle_{+\infty}
-
\big\langle
\mathcal{O}
\big\rangle_{-\infty}
\,&=\,
   e^{\{ \,\,\, , \Omega \}} \mathcal{O}
- \mathcal{O}
\,=\,
\{\mathcal{O},{\Omega}\}
+ \frac{1}{2!}\, \{\{\mathcal{O},{\Omega}\},{\Omega}\}
+ \cdots
\,.
\end{aligned}
</math>In both cases, the scattering generator acts on the observables as a Hamiltonian (thus in terms of right adjoint action). Note that the classical impulse formula
also follows by implementing the pullback by the inverse of the [[S-symplectomorphism|''S''-symplectomorphism]],
which maps functions on the final phase space to functions on the initial phase space.<ref name="PSFOR" /><ref name="KKKL" />

== Conventions and Terminology ==
Another prominent convention for the scattering generator uses the definition
<math>\hat{N} = -i\hbar \log\hat{S}</math>
and the name "''N''-matrix."<ref name=Damgaard/><ref name=2512.05017>
{{Cite journal
|last1=Brandhuber |first1=Andreas
|last2=Brown |first2=Graham R.
|last3=Pichini |first3=Paolo
|last4=Travaglini |first4=Gabriele
|last5=Matasan |first5=Pablo V.
|date=2025

|journal=Journal of High Energy Physics
|volume=2026
|issue=7
|page=151
|doi=10.1007/JHEP07(2026)151
|arxiv=2512.05017
|bibcode=2026JHEP...07..151B
}}</ref> Technically speaking,
the scattering generator should be distinguished from 
the [[Magnusian]],<ref name="MAGNUSIAN">
{{Cite journal 
|last1=Kim |first1=Jung-Wook
|last2=Patil |first2=Raj
|last3=Schoepner |first3=Trevor
|last4=Travaglini |first4=G.
|last5=Steinhoff Matasan |first5=Jan

}}</ref>
which is a broader term that can refer to the logarithm of time-evolution maps (not necessarily in scattering). A clarification has been made between the classical scattering generator, the eikonal phase, and the on-shell action.<ref name="MAGNUSIAN" />
